translations.title: Like a Flower in the Rain
translations.text:
I cut the nail of the middle finger

of my right hand

very short

and began rubbing her cunt

while she sat on the bed

putting cream on her arms

her face

and her breasts

after bathing.

Then she lit a cigarette:

‘you keep going,’

and she smoked, and kept putting on

cream.

I kept rubbing her cunt.

‘Do you want an apple?’ I asked her.

‘Okay,’ she said, ‘are you going to eat one?’

But it was her I ate…

she began to turn

then rolled onto her side,

she was getting wet and opening

like a flower in the rain.

Then she lay face down

and her most beautiful ass

translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Explicit language, repetitions, and the supplied line and stanza breaks are retained.

translations.title: Carefully Tuned to...
translations.text:
Carefully tuned to

the song of a fish

I was in the kitchen

halfway to madness

dreaming of Hemingway’s

Spain.

It’s muggy, as they say,

I can’t breathe,

I have shit and

read the sports pages,

I opened the refrigerator,

saw a piece of purple

meat

and put it back

there.

The place to find the center

is at the edge

that rattling in the sky

is only a pipe

vibrating.

Terrible things advance along the

walls; cancer flowers grow

on the porch; my white cat

had one eye torn out

and there are only 7 days left

of racing

in the summer season.

The dancer never came from the

Normandy Club

and Jimmy didn’t bring the

whore,

but there is a postcard from

Arkansas

and a returnable form from Food King:

10 free days in Hawaii,

all you have to do

is fill it out

but I don’t want to go to

Hawaii

I want the whore with pelican eyes

bronze navel

and

ivory heart.

I take out the piece of purple

meat,

throw it into the

pan.

Then the telephone rings.

I fall to one knee

and roll under

the table. I stay there

until it stops ringing.

Then I get up and

turn on

the radio.

No wonder Hemingway was

a drunk, goddamned Spain!

I can’t stand it

either.

It’s so terribly

muggy.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The slang, abrupt imagery, and supplied line and stanza breaks are retained.

translations.title: Freedom
translations.text:
he drank wine all night, that 28th,

and kept thinking about her;

the way she walked and talked and loved

the way she told him things that seemed true,

but weren’t, and he knew the color

of every one of her dresses,

and her shoes, he knew the rise and curve of every heel,

as well as the legs they shaped.


And she had gone out again when he came home, and

would return with that special stench, again

and so she did.


She came in around three in the morning

filthy as a shit-eating pig,

and he grabbed the butcher knife

and she screamed,

backing against the boardinghouse wall

still beautiful somehow,

even as love vanished.


That yellow dress,

his favorite,

and she screamed again.


And he took the knife

unbuckled his belt,

tore off his clothes in front of her,

and cut off his balls.


And he held them in his hands,

like walnuts

and dropped them into the toilet

and flushed.

and she kept screaming,

as the room turned red


OH GOD!

WHAT HAVE YOU DONE?


And he sat there,

holding three towels between his legs

no longer caring whether she left or stayed

whether she dressed in yellow or green

or anything else.


And while one hand held the towels,

he raised the other and poured himself more wine.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Graphic language, capitalization, and stanza structure are retained.

translations.title: Quiet Clean Girls in Nice Dresses
translations.text:
All the ones I know are whores, ex-whores,

madwomen. I see men with quiet,

kind women, I see them in supermarkets,

I see them walking the streets together,

I see them in their apartments: people at

peace, living together. I know their peace

is only partial, but there is

peace, often hours and days of peace.


All the ones I have known are addicted to pills,

alcoholics, whores, ex-whores, madwomen.

When one leaves

another arrives

worse than the one before.


I see so many men with quiet clean girls

well dressed

girls with faces that aren’t wolfish

or predatory.


‘Don’t bring another whore around here,’ I tell

my few friends, ‘I’ll fall in love with one.’


‘You couldn’t live with a good woman, Bukowski.’


I need a good woman,

I need a good woman,

more than I need this typewriter,

more than I need my car, more

than I need Mozart.


I need a good woman so badly that

I can taste her in the air, I can feel her

in my fingertips,

I can see sidewalks built

for her feet to walk on,

I can see pillows for her head,

I can feel my laughter waiting,

I can see her petting a cat,

I can see her sleeping,

I can see her slippers on the floor.


I know she exists

but where is she on this earth

while the whores keep arriving?
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Derogatory language, repetition, and stanza structure are retained.

translations.title: They Said Céline Was a Nazi...
translations.text:
They said Céline was a Nazi

they said Pound was a fascist

they said Hamsun was a Nazi and a fascist.

They put Dostoevsky before a firing squad

and they killed Lorca

they gave Hemingway electric shock treatments

(and you know he shot himself)

and they ran Villon out of town (Paris)

and Mayakovsky

disillusioned with the regime

and after a lovers’ quarrel,

well,

he shot himself too.

Chatterton took rat poison

and it worked

and some say Malcolm Lowry died

choking on his own vomit

drunk.

Crane threw himself into the ship’s

propellers or to the sharks.

Harry Crosby’s sun was black.

Berryman preferred the bridge.

Plath didn’t light the oven.

Seneca cut his wrists in the

bathtub (that’s the best way:

in warm water)

Thomas and Behan drank themselves

to death and

there are many more.

And you want to be a

writer?

It’s that kind of war:

creation kills,

many go mad,

some lose their way and

can never do it

again.

A few grow old.

A few make money.

Some starve to death (like Vallejo).

It’s that kind of war:

casualties everywhere.

All right, go ahead

do it

but when they attack you

from the side you can’t see

don’t come to me with

regrets.

Now I’m going to smoke a cigarette

in the bathtub

and then I’m going to go to

sleep.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Names, parenthetical remarks, and supplied line and stanza breaks are retained.

translations.title: Today the Blackbirds Are Restless
translations.text:
More alone than a dry exhausted orchard

set upon the earth

for use and abuse.

Downcast as an ex-boxer selling

newspapers on the corner.

Broken into tears like

a chorus girl grown old

receiving her final check.

A handkerchief will come in handy, your honor,

your grace.

Today the blackbirds are restless

like

ingrown toenails

on a night

in the cell…

wine moaned wine,

the blackbirds scamper and

flutter

repeating

melodies and Spanish castanets.

And anywhere is not

anywhere…

it is a dream worse than

tortillas or a flat tire:

why do we go on

with our heads and

pockets full of

dust

like a bad child just expelled

from school…

tell me

you who were a hero in some

revolution

you who teach children

you who drink calmly

you who own great houses

and stroll through gardens

you who have killed a man and possess a

beautiful wife

tell me

why I burn like an

old dry

dump.

We could keep up an interesting

correspondence.

We would keep the mailman busy.

And the butterflies and the ants and the bridges and

the cemeteries

the rocket builders and the dogs and the auto

mechanics

would continue

a little longer.

Until we ran out of stamps

and/or

ideas.

Don’t be ashamed of

anything; I suppose God thought of everything

even

the locks

on doors.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The surreal comparisons, direct address, and supplied spacing are retained.

translations.title: 3 Hours, 16 Minutes and 30 Seconds
translations.text:
I am supposed to be a great poet

and I am sleepy in the afternoon

I know death

is a gigantic bull

ready to charge me

and I am sleepy in the afternoon

I know there are wars and men fighting in the ring

I know there is good food, good wine, good women

and I am sleepy in the afternoon

I know there is a woman who loves me

and I am sleepy in the afternoon,

I lean toward the sun behind a yellow curtain

and I wonder:

Where have the summer flies gone?

I remember Hemingway’s bloody death

and I am sleepy in the afternoon.

Someday I won’t be sleepy in the afternoon

someday I will write a poem

that will set off volcanoes

in the hills out there

but right now I am sleepy in the afternoon

and someone asks me ‘Bukowski, what time is it?’

and I answer ‘3 hours, 16 minutes and 30 seconds.’

I feel very guilty,

I feel filthy, useless,

insane, I am sleepy

in the afternoons,

they are bombing churches,

well, that’s all right,

children ride ponies in the parks,

that’s all right,

libraries are full of thousands of wise books,

there is great music locked inside the radio

and I am sleepy in the afternoon,

I have a rumba inside me saying,

bah, let the others do it,

let them win,

let me sleep,

wit is in the dark

sweeping darkness like a broom,

I am going where the summer flies have gone,

try to catch me.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The refrain, quoted time, and supplied line and stanza breaks are retained.

translations.title: Nirvana
translations.text:
without much choice

and almost without meaning to,

he was a young man

on a bus

crossing North Carolina

headed

somewhere

and it began to snow

and the bus stopped

at a café

in the hills and

the passengers

went in.

he sat at the counter

with the others,

ordered and was

brought his food,

which was particularly good

as was the coffee.

The waitress was not

like the women he

had known.

She wasn’t putting on airs,

a natural humor flowed

from her.

The cook said

crazy things.

The dishwasher,

in back,

laughed

with a laugh

clean

and pleasant.

the young man watched

the snow through the

windows.

He wanted to stay

in that café

forever.

A strange feeling

flooded him:

that everything

was

beautiful

there,

that everything would always remain

beautiful

there.

then the driver

told the passengers

it was time to leave.

the young man

thought, I’ll stay

here, I’ll stay here.

But

he got up and followed

the others to

the bus.

He found his seat

and watched the café

through the window.

the bus started,

rounded a curve,

and went down the road,

away from the hills.

the young man

looked

ahead.

The other passengers

talked about other things

read

or

tried

to sleep.

they had not noticed

the magic.

the young man

rested his head

against the seat,

closed his eyes,

pretended

to sleep.

Nothing remained

but to listen to the

sound

of the engine,

the sound of the

wheels

in the snow.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Lowercase openings, spare lineation, and stanza spacing are retained.

translations.title: Claws of Paradise
translations.text:
Wooden butterfly

baking-soda smile

sawdust fly…

I like my belly

and the man at the liquor store

calls me

‘Mr. Schlutz.’

The racetrack cashiers

shout

‘THE POET KNOWS!’

when I cash my bets

the ladies

who get in and out of bed

say they love me

when I walk past them with

white wet feet.

Albatross with drunken eyes

Popeye’s dirty underwear

bedbugs of Paris,

I have saved the barricades

I have mastered

the automobile

the hangover

the tears

but I know

the final fate

like any schoolboy who watches

traffic crush

the cat as it passes.

My skull has a dent an

inch and a half long right at the

crown.

Most of my teeth are

in front,

I get dizzy in waves in supermarkets

I spit blood when I drink

whisky

and a sorrow comes over me

that grows into

pain

when I think of all the

good women I have known

who have dissolved

faded

into trivialities:

trips to Pasadena,

picnics with the children,

toothpaste caps

down the drain.

There is nothing to do

but drink

bet on the horses

bet on the poems

when the young girls

become women

and the machine guns

are aimed at me

crouched

behind walls thinner

than eyelids.

There is no defense

but all the mistakes

made.

Meanwhile

I shower

answer the telephone

make hard-boiled eggs

study movement and decay

and feel as good

as anyone

while I walk in the sun.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The surreal catalogue, capitalization, and supplied spacing are retained.

translations.title: Comments on My Latest Book of Poetry
translations.text:
You’re better than ever.

a piece of shit.

my mother hates you.

you’re rich.

you’re the best writer in the English language.

can I come see you?

I write like you, only better.

why do you drive a BMW?

why don’t you give readings anymore?

can you still get it up?

do you know Allen Ginsberg?

what do you think of Henry Miller?

would you write a foreword for my next book?

I’m sending you a photo of Céline.

I’m sending you my grandfather’s pocket watch.

the enclosed jacket was knitted by my wife in the Bavarian style.

did you get drunk with Mickey Rourke?

I’m a 19-year-old girl and I’m going to come clean your house.

you’re a stinking bastard for telling people Shakespeare is unreadable.

what do you think of Norman Mailer?

why do you steal from Hemingway?

why do you bash Tolstoy?

I’m in the can and as soon as I get out I’m coming to see you.

I think you lick ass.

you saved my fucking life.

why do you hate women?

I love you.

I read your poems at parties.

I saw you at the racetrack but I didn’t want to bother you.

I’d like to renew our relationship.

I can drink much more than you.

you stole it from Sherwood Anderson.

did you know Ezra?

I’m lonely and I think of you every night.

who the fuck do you think you’re fooling?

I don’t have much tit but I’ve got good legs.

translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. Lowercase presentation, explicit language, and the sequence of brief comments are retained.

translations.title: If It Doesn’t Come Bursting Out of You...
translations.text:
If it doesn’t come bursting out of you,

in spite of everything,

don’t do it.

Unless it comes unasked out of your heart

and your mind and your mouth

and your guts,

don’t do it.

If you have to sit for hours

staring at the computer screen

or hunched over your typewriter

searching for words,

don’t do it.

If you’re doing it for money or fame,

don’t do it.

If you’re doing it because you want women in your bed,

don’t do it.

If you have to sit

and rewrite it again and again,

don’t do it.

If just thinking about doing it wears you out,

don’t do it.

If you’re trying to write

like somebody else, forget it.


If you have to wait for it to roar out of you,

wait patiently.

If it never roars out of you, do something else.


If you first have to read it to your wife

or your girlfriend or your boyfriend

or your parents or to anybody at all,

you’re not ready.


Don’t be like so many writers,

don’t be like so many thousands of

people who call themselves writers,

don’t be dull and boring and pretentious,

don’t be consumed by self-love.

The libraries of the world

yawn themselves to sleep

over that kind of people.

Don’t be one of them.

Don’t do it.

Unless it comes out of your soul

like a rocket,

unless remaining still

would drive you to madness,

suicide or murder,

don’t do it.

Unless the sun inside you

is burning your guts, don’t do it.

When it is truly time,

and if you have been chosen,

it will happen by itself and

it will keep happening until you die

or until it dies in you.

There is no other way.

And there never was.
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The repeated imperative and supplied stanza structure are retained.

translations.title: Dinner 1933
translations.text:
When my father ate

his lips became

greasy

with the food

and while he ate

he talked about how

good the food was

and how

most people

didn’t eat

as well

as we did.

He liked

to wipe up

what was left

on the plate

with a piece of

bread,

while making

noises of approval

that sounded more like

grunts

he slurped the

coffee,

making a loud

bubbling

noise

and then

set down

the cup.

‘What’s for dessert,

Jell-O?’


My mother

brought it

in a large dish

and my father

served it

and as it fell onto the plate

the Jell-O made

a strange noise,

almost like

the sound of a

fart.


Then came

the whipped cream,

heaps of it

on the Jell-O.

‘mmm, Jell-O and

whipped cream!’

my father sucked the

Jell-O and whipped cream

off the spoon.

It sounded as if

he were entering

a streamlined

tunnel.

After finishing

that

he wiped his mouth

with an enormous white napkin,

rubbing hard

in circular

motions,

the napkin

almost hid

his entire

face

and after that

he took out

the Camel

cigarettes.

He lit one

with a wooden

kitchen match,

and then left

the match

still burning

in an ashtray,

then a sip

of coffee,

he set down the cup again

and took a good drag

on the Camel.

‘mmm, that meal

was good!’

Soon afterward

in my room,

lying on the bed

in the dark,

what I had

eaten

and what I had

seen

managed

to make me

sick.

The only

good thing

was

hearing

the crickets

outside.


Outside

in another world

where I

did not live.




‘Dinner,’ 1933
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version attributed to Charles Bukowski. The food sounds, brand name, closing source title, and supplied spacing are retained.

translations.title: Parting
translations.text:
It is foolish to lament,

Though we are doomed to part:

The only wisdom is to welcome

Someone’s memory in the heart:


We can dwell in the thoughts

That we ourselves have cultivated,

And roar with scorn and injured courage

Let the world do its worst.


We will not let its follies trouble us,

We will take them from whence they come;

And at the end of every day we’ll find

A merry laugh as home.


When we leave each friend and brother,

When far apart we are,

We will think of one another,

Even better than we were.


Every glorious sight above us,

Every pleasant sight below,

We will join with those who left us,

With those whom, even in death, we love still.


At sunset, when we sit

Alone beside the fire,

The warm and faithful heart

Will receive the same reward.


We may burn the bonds that bind us,

Woven by cold human hands,

There where no one dares defy us

We may meet in thought.


Therefore weeping is foolish,

Keep a merry spirit as you can;

And never doubt that Fate offers

A pleasant future for present pain.




‘Parting’
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Charlotte Brontë. The eight quatrains and closing source title are retained.

translations.title: Regret
translations.text:
Long ago I wished to leave

The house where I was born;

Long I used it but to grieve,

My home seemed forlorn,

Empty years in desolate halls,

Through the silent rooms

Stalking fears would prowl;

Now its memory spills onto pages

Where the ink is my tender tears.


I have known life and marriage.

Things that once were bright,

Now, like absolute deeds,

Float in every ray of light.

In the midst of life, that unknown sea,

No isle of blessing have I known;

At last, through the wild tempest

My sorrow was summoned home.


Farewell, dark and steep abyss!

Farewell, Foreign Lands!

Sweep, sweep the clouds from the sky,

Open your glorious realm of old!

Yet, when I had safely passed

That vexing and exhausting beginning,

A beloved voice, amid trembling and roaring,

Might summon me again.


Despite the brightness in the soul of an evening rose

In this Paradise rising over me,

William! Even from Heaven’s rest

I have turned my eyes, summoned by you.

This gathering storm will not restrain

My spirit, but will exalt it.

All my Heaven dwelt within your breast,

And only there will I find eternity.




‘Regret’
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Charlotte Brontë. The four stanzas, direct address to William, and closing source title are retained.

translations.title: An Echo from Willowwood
translations.text:
Two gazed intently at the waters, he looked and she,

Avoiding his hand, but with her heart close by,

Pale and uncertain on the water’s edge,

As at the brink of an unavoidable departure.

Each with eyes upon the other, she and he,

Each felt the hunger of the heart that leaps and sinks,

Each tasted the bitterness that both must drink,

There on the border of life’s sea.

Lilies on the surface, in the deep

Two melancholy faces yearn for one another,

Resolute and disinclined to speech:

A sudden ripple shook the faces,

For a moment joined them, and then they vanished:

Then those hearts were joined,

And thus were parted.




‘An Echo from Willowwood,’


1880
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Christina Rossetti. The single stanza, closing source title, and date are retained.

translations.title: Goblin Market
translations.text:
From morning until night

the goblins cry with all their might:

‘buy our fruits,

come, come and buy

quinces and apples,

lemons and oranges

plump cherries,

melons and strawberries,

rosy peaches,

wild blueberries

dark mulberries,

deep-purple blackberries,

pineapples and wild pears,

apricots and raspberries;

all reaching ripeness

together in summer;

morning arrives

and evening slips away,

buy what summer leaves:

fresh grapes from the vine,

pomegranates lovely and full,

dates and pears,

monk’s plums and greengages,

damsons too and egg plums,

come and taste them, don’t be shy:

raisins and currants,

scarlet berries,

figs in abundance

southern citrus,

sweet and fresh:

buy, stretch out your hand.’




‘Goblin Market’
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish excerpt of Christina Rossetti. The fruit catalogue, invitation, and closing source title are retained.

translations.title: Dreamland
translations.text:
Where sunless rivers weep,

Pouring their waves into the deep,

She sleeps an enchanted sleep

From which she will not wake.

Led by a wandering star,

She came from places far,

Seeking her pleasures

Where the shadows lie.


She left the rosy morning,

She left the fields of corn

For the cold twilight

And languid springs.

Through sleep, as through a veil,

She watches the pale sky,

Listening to the airy song

Of the sad nightingale.


Rest, rest, a perfect rest

Covers her brow and breasts,

Her face is turned toward the west,

Toward the Purple Land.

She cannot see the grain,

Ripening on hill and plain,

She cannot feel the rain

Fall upon her fragile hand.


Rest, rest forever

On the lush shores

Rest until the heart is still,

Until the core of time dies.

Sleep a sleep that sorrow

Cannot disturb,

Night will not be broken by morning,

Until joy takes possession

Of her perfect peace.




‘Dreamland’
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Christina Rossetti. The four stanzas, repetitions, and closing source title are retained.

translations.title: A Portrait
translations.text:
She gave up her beauty in tender youth,

Gave up hope, and cheerful ways;

She veiled her eyes from forbidden vanity,

And chose the bitterest of truth.

Hard on herself, and toward others merciful,

Servant of servants, few certainties to praise,

Long prayers and fasts in the hermitage, night and day:

She schooled herself in coarse sights and sounds,

Since with the poor she had to dwell, with ravaged workers,

Until the lowliest of all things made

Should be satisfied: She herself renouncing her being,

Counting earthly goods with sorrow.

Then, with the calm of her choice, she bore the cross

And hated the world for love of God.


They knelt in anguished silence beside her bed,

She could not weep; but calmly there she lay.

All pain had left her, and the final ray of sun

Shone through her, dyeing the somber curtains red.

In her heart, She said:

Heaven opens; I leave the world and go far away,

The Bridegroom calls me—shall the Bride refuse?

Then upon her breast she bowed her head.

O Lily, gem of priceless worth,

O dove of patient gaze and tender voice,

O fruitful vine amid the barren earth,

O maiden filled with love and purity,

Bow your head before your earthly friends,

To rise with the saints in Paradise.




‘A Portrait’
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Christina Rossetti. Religious imagery, capitalization, two-stanza structure, and closing source title are retained.

translations.title: A Frog’s Fate
translations.text:
Scorning her home in the village

And the village pond,

An imposing Frog despised every path

Hopping down the imperial road.


Neither fierce pig nor barking dog

Could disconcert so majestic a Frog.

The morning dew still lingered,

Her sides grew cold, her tongue went numb:

When night should have come, the dew came first,

And was rejected by our pilgrim Frog.


But, alas! The roadside grass conceals her

She is no longer seen hopping.

Unawares a broad cart rolled

That crushed her, ran over her joys, her charms.

And from drowning death a feeble song arose

Breaking the Frog’s perpetual silence:

You buoyant Frogs, you small and great,

Even I am mortal after all!

My road to fame became a road of mud;

I perish on the dreadful highway;

Ah, my old familiar way!


The drowning Frog sobbed and departed;

The Charioteer strode whistling past,

Unaware of the infamous slaughter,

Whistling the Charioteer crossed,

Whistling (one might say)

As frogs whistle their courtship.

A hypothetical frog run over,

Ignorant of reality.


O rich and poor, O great and small,

Such carelessness shakes us.

A shattered Frog endures it all,

A Frog as insignificant as absolute:

That hypothetical and solitary Frog

Is the Frog upon which we dwell.




‘A Frog’s Fate’
translations.editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish version of Christina Rossetti. Capitalized Frog and Charioteer, five-stanza structure, and closing source title are retained.

translations.title: Work
translations.text:
This
		others did

better than you

for centuries.

On them depended

your sense of freedom


your clean shirt

and the leisure of your reading and writing.

On
		them depends


everything

that seemed natural to you

like going to the movies

or being
	\tslightly sad.


What is natural, however, is mud,

sweat, excrement.


From there begins

the epic, which is not only

a
		mat­ter of dazzling heroes,


but also

of obscure heroes, ground beneath your steps,

page
		where words are written.


Leave words behind, try

a little

what they did,
		do,


will keep doing

so that you may be:

they,

those sunk in
		necessity


and gravitation,

those ground down by relentless suns

so
		that your bread may always be fresh,


those bound

to the iron post of monotony

so that you may
		shuffle every theme,


those maimed

by a mechanical gesture infinitely repeated


		so that you may do


whatever you please with your soul and your body.

Reduce yourself like
		them.


Taste the oven,

eat fatigue.

Enter a little, even if
		clandestinely,


into the terrible realm of those who sustain

life.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish poem by Cintio Vitier. Indentation, stanza structure, and the address to the reader are retained.
